name: Debiasing
statement: Cognitive biases can be reduced by teaching people about them, and the teaching is said to carry across to new problems and to hold for months.
meaning: Debiasing is a research programme rather than a bias. Its claim is that the errors catalogued elsewhere in this corpus are correctable, and that a person can be taught to make fewer of them. Baruch Fischhoff's 1982 chapter set the frame the later work still uses. A bias may sit in the judge, in the task, or in the mismatch between the two, and each source calls for a different repair. For a faulty judge the chapter proposes an escalation: warn that the bias exists, describe its direction, give personalised feedback, then coach and train. Sellier, Scopelliti and Morewedge list those four steps, and this entry takes them from that description rather than from the chapter itself. Two questions decide whether any of it works. Does the gain appear on a problem the trainee was never drilled on, and is it still there weeks later.

origin.where: Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases, Cambridge University Press
origin.note: The chapter runs from page 422 to 444 and is the citation the training literature returns to. Its text could not be obtained for this entry, so nothing here is quoted from it. Morewedge and colleagues call the start it describes rocky.

evidence: Morewedge and colleagues ran the two experiments the modern claim rests on. Everyone was trained. Each person was randomly assigned to play a computer game or to watch a 30-minute video. Both groups filled in a bias-commission scale before training and again straight after. A third scale followed online, eight weeks later in Experiment 1 and twelve weeks later in Experiment 2. Experiment 1 covered bias blind spot, confirmation bias and the fundamental attribution error, with 243 people finishing the laboratory session and 196 the follow-up. Overall bias fell for the game, d pre-post = 1.68 and d pre-followup = 1.11, and for the video, 0.69 and 0.66. Experiment 2 covered anchoring, projection and representativeness, with 238 in the laboratory and 192 at follow-up, and both were large: game 1.74 and 1.16, video 1.75 and 1.07. The confirmation-bias scale tested six facets and the game taught three. At follow-up the untrained facets sat at d = 0.65 and the trained ones at 0.24, a gap the paper reports as not significant, t < 1. Sellier, Scopelliti and Morewedge took the same game into a business school. Two hundred and ninety graduate students at HEC Paris solved an unannounced case modelled on the Challenger launch, some before their training session and some after. Trained students picked the inferior hypothesis-confirming option 58.8% of the time against 72.2% untrained, Wald chi-square(1) = 5.23, p = .022, odds ratio 0.549, 95% CI [0.33, 0.92]. Chang, Chen, Mellers and Tetlock randomly assigned forecasters in four nine-month geopolitical tournaments to a training module of under an hour or to none. Mean Brier scores improved by 10% and 11% in year 1, 12% in year 2, 6% in year 3 and 7% in year 4, and trained forecasters led controls at both the start and the end of each year. Heerma van Voss and colleagues ran a preregistered test on 56 national risk analysts and 116 masters students, using a 15-minute scripted lecture and a group case, about 40 minutes in all. Confirmation bias fell in both groups, F(1, 168) = 104.579, partial eta-squared = 0.384 in the general domain and F(1, 168) = 45.999, partial eta-squared = 0.215 in the risk domain, with no difference between analysts and students.

replication.headline: Scores move on the tasks that were trained, and the pooled estimate from randomised trials is about a fifth of what the best-known single studies report.
replication.detail: Swaryandini and colleagues pooled 54 randomised trials of debiasing teaching in education, holding 383 effect sizes and 10,941 participants. On the likelihood of committing a bias the estimate is g = 0.26, 95% CI [0.14, 0.39], p < 0.001, from 160 effects in 41 studies. Their abstract records that every trial carried unclear or high risk of bias and that there was some risk of publication bias; the figures behind that judgement sit behind the paywall and were not obtained here. Medicine reaches a similar number from a separate literature. Staal and colleagues pooled 29 studies of cognitive reasoning tools covering 2,732 medical students and physicians and found Hedges' g = 0.28, 95% CI [0.14, 0.43], p < 0.001, with I-squared = 70%. Dropping three studies that had trained participants on the tool beforehand cut heterogeneity to 38% and the estimate to 0.20, 95% CI [0.10, 0.29]. That funnel plot is the one place publication bias has been tested at first hand in the sources read here, and Egger's regression found no asymmetry, t(27) = 1.84, p = 0.077. GRADE rated the evidence moderate, downgraded because only one of the studies had a prespecified analysis plan. Against those pooled figures sit single-laboratory results above d = 1.6. The disagreement is about size, not direction.

limits: Durability is the thinnest part of the record. Morewedge's follow-ups at eight and twelve weeks are the only planned retests among the studies read here. Sellier's long interval fell out of the timetable rather than the design. It allowed 57 students trained 43 to 52 days before the case to be set against 125 trained within 11 days. The confirming option went to 63.2% of the first group and 56.8% of the second, chi-square(1) = 0.65, p = .419. Chang's tournaments ran nine months each with training at the start. Heerma van Voss measured immediately after a 40-minute session and never again. Design is the second weakness. Morewedge assigned every participant to training and compared each group against its own pretest, which leaves retesting and practice on the scales tangled with the intervention. Heerma van Voss did the same. Sellier's assignment came from when each student signed up for a session rather than from the experimenters, and the paper answers that with robustness checks against selection rather than with randomisation. Chang did randomise, and its module taught more than debiasing. An analysis of the ten CHAMPS KNOW principles tied the probabilistic ones to accuracy, F = 11.96, p < 0.001, and the political ones to nothing, F = 0.08, p = 0.783. Most outcomes are bias scales built by the people who built the training. Swaryandini's abstract raises the same worry about depth and transfer beyond the classroom.
misreadings: The best-known figure in this literature has already been corrected. The published version of Sellier, Scopelliti and Morewedge says trained participants were 29% less likely to pick the inferior solution, the abstract now carried by PubMed says 19%, and Psychological Science ran a corrigendum at 31(6), 762. The underlying percentages are 58.8% against 72.2%. A second confusion treats consider-the-opposite as the same thing as debiasing training. Lord, Lepper and Preston's manipulation is a prompt inside a task rather than a course, and their abstract credits Francis Bacon with the original observation. What it reports is that considering the opposite corrected more than instructions to be as fair and unbiased as possible did. Third, the medical literature does not simply agree with the laboratory one. Sherbino, Kulasegaram, Howey and Norman taught cognitive forcing strategies to 145 students against 46 controls. A second diagnosis was sought by 52% of the trained and 48% of the controls, chi-square = 0.13, p = 0.91. The uncommon diagnosis was found by 45% in each group, chi-square = 0.001, p = 0.98. Their conclusion is that the interventions failed to show any reduction in diagnostic error by novices. Fourth, and this bears on the bias blind spot entry in this corpus, thinking oneself unbiased appears to blunt the training. Heerma van Voss and colleagues write that the bias blind spot reduces the efficacy of debiasing interventions, citing Scopelliti's work rather than reporting it themselves. Their own analysts showed as much blind spot as the students, both before the session and after it.
